title: Star-studded cluster
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6440, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6440 · constellation Sagittarius · about 28000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, P. FreireAcknowledgement: M. Cadelano and C. Pallanca

recognition.text: Ranked #72 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A round swarm of stars fills this Webb view, with a tight knot of bright white stars at its center, larger yellow stars scattered across the frame, and many stars showing spiky diffraction patterns against black space. This is NGC 6440, a globular cluster roughly 28,000 light-years away in Sagittarius, first discovered by William Herschel.

Globular clusters are roughly spherical, tightly bound groups of old stars. NGC 6440 is massive and rich in metals, and it formed and still orbits inside the Galactic bulge, the dense, near-spherical crowd of old stars in the Milky Way's inner region.

Webb's near-infrared camera was used to study the cluster's stars and its pulsars, rapidly spinning, strongly magnetized neutron stars whose beams sweep past us as pulses. The data give the first evidence from Webb of varying helium and oxygen abundances among a globular cluster's stars. Heavy crowding and reddening by interstellar dust had put such bulge clusters out of reach of other telescopes.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.84 x 1.18 arcminutes) and distance (28000 light years), the frame spans roughly 15 × 9.6 light-years. Its light set out about 28,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with the shortest-wavelength filter shown in blue, two middle filters in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes more easily through the interstellar dust that reddens and dims this cluster in visible light.

explore: Globular clusters hold hundreds of thousands to millions of stars, on average about one light-year apart, though they can be packed as tightly as the span of our Solar System. The fastest known pulsars spin more than 716 times per second, and in theory one could reach 1500 before losing energy or breaking apart.
alt: A spherical cluster of stars filling the frame, with bright white stars concentrated at the center, larger yellow stars scattered around, and diffraction spikes on many stars against a black background.
